summary: RPID adds optional elements to the Presence Information Data Format (PIDF) that give richer information about a presentity and its contacts. Much of it can be derived automatically, for example from calendars. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: PIDF, the format used to publish presence information, can say only that a service is open or closed. RPID adds optional XML elements to that format: what the person is doing, what mood they are in, what the place is like, whether a call would be private, and whether the device has been used recently. A watcher can use these values to decide how to reach the person.

subtitle: Optional XML elements that let a presence document say what a person is doing, where they are and how best to reach them.

tldr.problem: PIDF can only say whether a service is open or closed, give a contact URI and carry a note for a human to read. That is too little for software to judge whether a communication attempt is appropriate.
tldr.mechanism: RPID adds optional elements for persons, services (tuples) and devices, such as activities, mood, place, privacy and user-input. Many of them are chosen so they can be derived automatically from calendars, devices or sensors.
tldr.outcome: An RPID document stays a valid PIDF document, so PIDF-only watchers and gateways keep working, without the extra detail. Because the data can be highly sensitive, systems should let users reveal it selectively.

today: RFC 4480 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2006. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it is still the definition of the rich presence extension to PIDF.

sections.title: Purpose and Goals of RPID
sections.content:
The Presence Information Data Format (PIDF), defined in RFC 3863, describes a basic presence information format encoded in XML for systems that follow the common model for presence and instant messaging. It consists of a <presence> root element, zero or more <tuple> elements carrying presence information including a URI for communication, zero or more <note> elements, and zero or more extension elements from other namespaces. Each tuple defines a basic status of either open or closed.

It is frequently useful to convey additional information about a user that has to be interpreted by a program, and is therefore not appropriate for the <note> element, which is typically intended for the human observer. This document defines the extensions that carry such information, and calls them the Rich Presence Information Data format, RPID.

The presence data model in RFC 4479 models the state of a presentity with three data elements: service, device and person. Services are encoded with the <tuple> element, devices and persons with the <device> and <person> elements. Neither PIDF nor the data model defines presence attributes beyond the <basic> status element, so RPID adds attributes that describe those three data elements.

The document states two goals. The first is to provide rich presence information that is at least as powerful as common commercial presence systems, which simplifies the move to systems complying with the Common Profile for Instant Messaging. The second is to maintain backward compatibility with PIDF, so that PIDF-only watchers and gateways keep working properly without access to the new functionality.

The document makes no assumptions about how the information is generated. Because users are not always diligent about updating their presence status, the extensions are chosen so that much of the information can be derived automatically from other sources, such as personal calendars, the status of communication devices, typing activity and physical presence detectors. Many of the elements correspond to data found in personal calendars, so some were aligned with calendar formats such as iCal in RFC 2445.

A presence document can be generated by a single entity or composed from information published by several. The presence server may compose, translate or filter the published state before delivering customized information to a watcher, for example by merging information from several user agents, removing whole elements or translating values. Since RPID is a PIDF XML document, it uses the content type application/pidf+xml.
sections.plainLanguage: PIDF publishes a small amount of information: a service is open or closed, here is a URI to reach it, and here is a note for a person to read. RPID adds machine-readable fields to the same document. Its two goals are to match what commercial presence systems offer and to leave plain PIDF documents working unchanged.

sections.title: The Element Set and the Document Structure
sections.content:
Some RPID elements describe services, some devices and some the person, so they extend <tuple>, <device> or <person> respectively. The document defines these elements: <activities>, which enumerates what the person is doing; <class>, an identifier that groups similar person elements, devices or services; <deviceID>, which references the device that contributes to the service described by a tuple; <mood>; <place-is>, which reports properties of the current place such as levels of light and noise; <place-type>; <privacy>; <relationship>; <service-class>; <sphere>; <status-icon>; <time-offset>; and <user-input>.

Table 1 in the document records, for each element, whether it can take from and until attributes, whether it can include a <note> element, and in which of the <person>, <tuple> and <device> elements it may appear.

The elements marked in the from/until column MAY be qualified with those attributes to describe the absolute time when the element assumed its value and the absolute time until which it is expected to be valid. There can be several elements of the same type, and their time ranges SHOULD NOT overlap. Elements MAY contain an id attribute that allows the element to be referenced uniquely.

The namespace for the elements is the URN urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:pidf:rpid. Enumerations can be extended with elements from other namespaces, and the <activities>, <mood> and <place-type> elements can also carry an <other> element with free text for application-specific values. All elements described in the document are optional within PIDF documents.

The document also notes that a presentity is unlikely to publish all of these elements at once, and that there is no guarantee the information is accurate, because users forget to update calendars or do not adjust presence information by hand. Where free text is used, the elements SHOULD be labelled with the xml:lang attribute, and if it is absent the default is i-default. Since RPID is XML, it supports Unicode and its compact UTF-8 encoding, and use of UTF-8 is RECOMMENDED where parser encoding support may be inconsistent.
sections.plainLanguage: Each RPID element belongs to the person, to one service or to one device, and the document lists exactly where each one may appear. Elements that change over time can carry a start and an end time. Every element is optional, so a document can use as many or as few as the publisher wants.

sections.title: Person Elements: Activities, Mood and Place
sections.content:
The <activities> element describes what the person is currently doing, as an enumeration of activity elements. A person can be engaged in several activities at once, for example traveling and having a meal. The enumeration draws on elements such as appointment, away, breakfast, busy, dinner, holiday, in-transit, looking-for-work, lunch, meal, meeting, on-the-phone, other, performance, permanent-absence, playing, presentation, shopping, sleeping, spectator, steering, travel, tv, unknown, vacation, working and worship. If a person publishes an activity of permanent-absence, it is likely that all services report a status of closed. Activities such as appointment, breakfast, dinner, holiday, lunch, meal, meeting, performance, travel and vacation can often be derived from calendar information.

The <mood> element describes the mood of the presentity, with the mood given as the name of a child element such as <happy/>; one such child element is REQUIRED, and a natural-language description in a <note> child is OPTIONAL. The document recommends implementing the mood values proposed in Jabber Extension JEP-0107, which is a superset of the Wireless Village mood values and of the values in the Affective Knowledge Representation defined by Lisetti. The list includes afraid, amazed, angry, annoyed, anxious, ashamed, bored, brave, calm, cold, confused, contented, cranky, curious, depressed, disappointed, disgusted, distracted, embarrassed, excited, flirtatious, frustrated, grumpy, guilty, happy, hot, humbled, humiliated, hungry, hurt, impressed, in_awe, in_love, indignant, interested, invincible, jealous, lonely, mean, moody, nervous, neutral, offended, other, playful, proud, relieved, remorseful, restless, sad, sarcastic, serious, shocked, shy, sick, sleepy, stressed, surprised, thirsty, unknown and worried.

The <place-is> element describes properties of the place the person is at, which tells the watcher what kind of communication is likely to succeed. Each major media type has its own attributes. For audio they are noisy, ok, quiet and unknown; for video toobright, ok, dark and unknown; for text uncomfortable, inappropriate, ok and unknown. Omitting the element indicates that the property is unknown.

The <place-type> element describes the type of place the person is at, such as a classroom or a home. Its initial set of values is contained in the Location Types Registry in RFC 4589, and that list can be augmented with free text or with additional IANA-registered values.
sections.plainLanguage: Three elements describe the person. Activities lists what the person is doing, from a fixed list such as away, busy, meeting or sleeping, and a calendar can supply many of them. Mood names a feeling such as happy or anxious. Place-is rates the surroundings for audio, video and text, and place-type names the kind of place it is.

sections.title: Service, Device and Contact Elements
sections.content:
The <privacy> element indicates which types of communication third parties in the vicinity of the presentity are unlikely to be able to intercept accidentally or intentionally. It does not describe the privacy properties of the electronic communication channel, such as the encryption algorithm or the network protocol used. Its values are audio, for communications that inappropriate individuals are not likely to overhear; text, for text communications they are not likely to see; video, for video communications they are not likely to see; and unknown, when the information is not known. The element can be used by logic running on the watcher, or by a composer, to filter, sort and label tuples. For example, a composer may hold rules that limit publication of tuples labeled private to a select subset of the watchers.

The <class> element describes the class of the service, device or person. Several elements can share a class name, but each person, service or device has only one class label, and the naming is left to the presentity. A presence agent can use it for filtering or authorization. It MUST NOT be qualified with from and until attributes.

The <deviceID> element in a tuple references the device that provides that service. One service can be provided by multiple devices, so a tuple may contain zero or more of them, and the order carries no meaning. It MUST NOT be qualified with from and until attributes.

The <relationship> element extends the tuple and designates the type of relationship an alternate contact has with the presentity. It is provided only if the tuple refers to somebody other than the presentity, and its values include family, friend, associate, assistant, supervisor, self and unknown, with self as the default. When a relationship is indicated, the URI in the <contact> element refers to the entity with the relationship, such as the assistant, not to the presentity itself.

The <service-class> element designates the type of service offered: electronic, postal, courier, freight, in-person or unknown. Electronic service is implied if the element is omitted, and the types postal, courier, freight and in-person MUST NOT be used unless the contact URI is empty. The contact URI of a tuple labeled with a relationship can hold a communication URI such as im, sip, sips, h323, tel or mailto, or a presence URI such as pres or sip.

The <sphere> element designates the current state and role the person plays, for example work mode, home, or an activity related to another organization. The document defines names only for work, home and unknown. Spheres let a person switch rules that depend on which groups of people should learn about their status, so a leader of a scout troop who sets the sphere to scouting can let fellow scoutmasters see the status and lose that access when switching to work or home.

The <status-icon> element holds a URI pointing to an image representing the current status, and a watcher MAY use it in a graphical user interface. Presentities SHOULD provide images in sizes and aspect ratios suitable for rendering as an icon, and support for JPEG, PNG and GIF formats is RECOMMENDED. Watchers resolving the URI MUST validate whether the local copy of the icon is current, using the standard cache control mechanism of the retrieval protocol.

The <time-offset> element gives the number of minutes of offset from UTC at the person's current location. A positive number means the local time of day is ahead of Universal Time, a negative number means it is behind. An optional description attribute can label the time zone for human readers. Publishers on mobile devices SHOULD NOT publish this information unless they know it reflects the current location, and SHOULD update it whenever they discover that the offset has changed.

The <user-input> element records the user-input or usage state of a service or device, based on human input such as a keyboard, pointing device or voice. In a <person> element it summarizes user input activity across all services and devices, generally reflecting the most recent input. It has two values, active or idle, with an optional last-input attribute recording when the last input was received and an optional idle-threshold element recording how long the presentity waits before reporting the service or device idle, measured in seconds. A two-state model was chosen because otherwise repeated last-input updates would be needed during continuous activity. Configuration MUST include the option to omit the last-input attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: Other elements describe the service, the device or the contact. A tuple can say which relationship a contact has to the person, what kind of service it is, whether the person is at work or at home, when the device was last used, and whether people nearby are likely to overhear or see the communication.

sections.title: XML Schema Definitions
sections.content:
The document publishes an XML Schema for the RPID namespace. Because of limitations in composing schemas, not all XML documents that validate against the schema are semantically valid RPID documents. In particular, the schema allows each element to appear anywhere in PIDF or data-model elements, while Table 1 restricts where these elements may appear in a semantically valid RPID document. Elements that do not have from and until parameters MUST NOT appear more than once in each <person>, <tuple> or <device>.

The schema defines each element as a complex type. The enumerations are restricted lists of empty elements, and elements such as <user-input> are simple content extending a base type, in that case the two values active and idle, with the idle-threshold and last-input attributes. The <time-offset> element extends an integer base with the description attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: The document ships a machine-readable schema for the new elements. The schema is looser than the document itself: it lets an element appear in more places than the rules allow, so a parser that only checks the schema can accept a document that the specification does not consider valid.

sections.title: Example Presence Document
sections.content:
The example describes the presentity pres:someone@example.com, which has a SIP contact, sip:someone@example.com, representing a service, and a device contact given as an email box. The presentity is in a meeting in a public office setting, and the until information indicates that this lasts until 5:30 pm local time. The presentity also has an assistant, sip:secretary@example.com, who happens to be available for communications.

The document has one tuple for the instant messaging service, one for the assistant, and one for the email service. The assistant tuple has no <status> element of its own beyond the basic open value and a mailto: contact with priority 1.0. The email tuple carries a <class> of email, a service class of electronic and a <status-icon> pointing at a PNG image. The <person> element carries activities qualified with from and until times, a mood of angry with a free-text mood of brooding, a place-is element reporting that audio conditions are noisy, a place type of residence, a privacy value of unknown, a sphere of bowling league, a status icon and a time offset of -240.
sections.plainLanguage: The worked example shows one presence document with three service tuples, one device and one person. The person element shows how the values fit together, with an activity that has a start and an end time, a mood, the noise level of the room, the type of place and the offset from UTC.

sections.title: Extending RPID and Registering Namespaces
sections.content:
Any developer can introduce their own element names, avoiding conflict by choosing an appropriate namespace URI. To add new standardized elements to the <activities>, <mood>, <privacy>, <relationship> and <service-class> enumerations, the extension process described in PIDF is followed, using namespace designators such as urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:pidf:ext, where ext is the name of the extension. New values for the <place-type> element are assigned according to RFC 4589 and given a namespace designator at the time of registration.

To avoid the unnecessary proliferation of XML namespaces containing a single element, groups of element registrations for each enumeration, such as <privacy>, SHOULD be bundled into a single namespace rather than assigning a new namespace to each new element.

The IANA considerations register the URN sub-namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:pidf:rpid for the elements defined by the document, and register the schema urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:pidf:status:rpid, pointing at the schema in Section 5. The document does not need a new content type; it inherits application/pidf+xml from PIDF.
sections.plainLanguage: New values can be added later without breaking anything. Anyone may define extra elements in a namespace of their own, and new values for the standard enumerations are registered under a namespace such as the PIDF extension namespace, with several values sharing one namespace rather than one namespace each.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of PIDF apply, as do those of the presence event package in RFC 3856. Compared with PIDF, this presence document format reveals additional information about presentities that can be highly sensitive. Beyond the traditional measures that protect confidentiality and integrity, systems should offer a means to selectively reveal information to particular watchers and to inspect the information being published, particularly when it is generated automatically from other sources such as calendars or sensors.

The document also notes that, like any reference to an external object, the <status-icon> may allow the presentity to induce the watcher to retrieve data from a third party, which it calls a content indirection attack. The result is either that harmful content is retrieved or that the load on the referenced server grows.
sections.plainLanguage: RPID reveals more about a person than PIDF does, and some of it is sensitive. Systems should let a user choose who sees which parts and let them review what is published, especially when the values come from a calendar or a sensor. The icon element can also make a watcher fetch an image from a third party, which is a way to attack that server.
